mechanisms.kill: The antioxidant that keeps your cells from going rancid
mechanisms.figure_alt: A fatty cell membrane: intact on the left, guarded at its centre by selenium, gone rancid with a visible age spot on the right.

beats.title: Your cells are fat
beats.text: Every cell and every mitochondrion is wrapped in a membrane made of fat — and fat oxidizes, goes rancid, the same way cooking oil does once it's heated or left out.
beats.hook: The rancidity that spoils oil in the pan can happen inside your own cell walls.

beats.title: The most efficient antioxidant
beats.text: Selenium — working through the glutathione-peroxidase enzyme system — is, in Wallach's telling, the most efficient antioxidant there is, standing guard over those fatty membranes right at the subcellular level.
beats.hook: A trace mineral you need in millionths of a gram is the bodyguard on every membrane you own.

beats.title: Rancid, made visible
beats.text: Pull selenium out and the fats peroxidize — the brown-gold residue (ceroid lipofuscin) surfaces on skin as "age spots" or "liver spots," while selenium-starved heart muscle can fail outright, as in Keshan disease and the sudden collapse of young athletes.
beats.hook: An age spot is rancid fat you can see — Wallach reads it as a warning, not a blemish.
